title: Reassessment Notice Issued Three Days Late Is Void, Not Curable: ITAT Delhi
meta_description: ITAT Delhi quashes a reassessment based on a Section 148 notice issued just three days after the six-year limitation period had expired.
court: Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Delhi Bench
case_name: Ravindra Sahu v. Income Tax Officer
citation: ITA No. 161/DEL/2026 (quantum) and ITA No. 162/DEL/2026 (penalty), Assessment Year 2015-16
body: Three days rarely decides a tax case, but it was enough to sink an entire reassessment against Ravindra Sahu for assessment year 2015-16. The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal's Delhi Bench found that the notice reopening his assessment had been issued just three days after the six-year limitation period for reassessment had already run out, and that was that.

The reopening itself followed a familiar pattern. The Assessing Officer had information about cash deposits in Sahu's bank account and issued a notice under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to reassess his income for the year on that basis. What the Assessing Officer apparently did not check closely enough was the calendar. By the time the notice went out, the six-year window within which a reassessment notice for that assessment year could validly be issued had already closed, by a margin of three days.

Before reaching that limitation point at all, the Tribunal had to clear a procedural hurdle of Sahu's own making. His appeal against the reassessment had reached the National Faceless Appeal Centre 543 days late, a delay substantial enough that condonation was far from automatic. The Tribunal accepted Sahu's explanation that the delay stemmed from a bona fide error rather than deliberate neglect, and condoned it, which meant the substantive challenge to the reassessment could actually be heard rather than being thrown out on a separate limitation point of its own.

On the merits of the time-bar itself, the Tribunal treated the three-day overshoot as fatal rather than a technicality to be waved through. A notice issued under Section 148 beyond the statutory limitation period is not a defect that can be cured by the Assessing Officer having acted in good faith or by the underlying information about cash deposits being credible on its own terms. The limitation period is jurisdictional: once it expires, the Assessing Officer simply has no power left to issue a valid reopening notice, however strong the case for reassessment might otherwise have looked.

Because the defect went to jurisdiction rather than to some curable procedural lapse, the Tribunal did not send the matter back to the CIT(A) or the National Faceless Appeal Centre for a fresh look. It allowed Sahu's appeals outright, covering both the quantum addition and the connected penalty, on the straightforward logic that there was nothing left to remand once the notice founding the entire reassessment was void from the start. A reassessment built on a notice with no jurisdictional basis cannot be rescued by sending the file back down for the lower authorities to try again on the same notice.

The penalty appeal fell with the quantum appeal for the same reason, rather than on any independent assessment of whether a penalty would otherwise have been justified. A penalty order under the Income Tax Act is parasitic on a valid underlying assessment or reassessment; once the reassessment itself is void for want of jurisdiction, there is no surviving addition left for a penalty to attach to, and the Tribunal did not need to examine the penalty on its own separate merits to say so.

Assessing Officers working against the six-year limitation window on reassessment notices should treat this ruling as a reminder that there is no margin for calendar error once an asset or cash-deposit allegation triggers a reopening. For taxpayers on the receiving end of a reassessment notice that looks like it may be arriving close to the edge of the limitation period, checking the exact date against the statutory six-year mark, down to the day, is worth doing before assuming the notice has to be answered on its merits at all.

The condonation of Sahu's own 543-day delay before the National Faceless Appeal Centre is worth separate attention for practitioners, since it shows the Tribunal was willing to look past a substantial lapse on the taxpayer's side once it accepted the explanation offered as a bona fide error rather than deliberate neglect. That willingness mattered here because it meant the time-barred notice argument actually got decided on its merits, rather than being shut out by a procedural default of Sahu's own making before the Tribunal ever reached the limitation question that decided the case in the end.
why_it_matters: A reassessment notice issued even a few days after the statutory limitation period expires is void for want of jurisdiction, not a curable defect, and the Tribunal will not remand such a case for fresh adjudication. Taxpayers facing a reassessment notice that arrives close to the six-year mark should check the exact date of issue against the limitation period before responding on the merits, since a time-barred notice can end the proceeding outright.
card_summary: ITAT Delhi quashes a reassessment against Ravindra Sahu for AY 2015-16, holding that a Section 148 notice issued three days after the six-year limitation period is void and not curable.
card_tip: Check the exact issue date of a Section 148 reassessment notice against the six-year limitation deadline; even a few days' delay makes the notice void for want of jurisdiction, not merely irregular.
verification_notes: The assessee's name, the appeal numbers, the assessment year, the basis for reopening (cash deposits), the three-day overshoot of the six-year limitation period, the 543-day delay before the National Faceless Appeal Centre and its condonation on grounds of bona fide error, and the Tribunal's decision to allow the appeals outright rather than remand are confirmed across Taxscan and the SAG Infotech blog. The order was reported as pronounced in open court on 19 August 2026, which this article uses as the decision date; the names of the Tribunal members were not confirmed in the sources reviewed.
